edbDesc: The pitch heard from tapping a cup of hot liquid rises after addition of a soluble powder. May be observed by stirring chocolate powder into a mug of hot milk, tapping bottom of mug with a spoon while milk is in motion. Pitch of the taps will increase progressively. Subsequent stirring decreases the pitch. Due to the effect of bubble density on the speed of sound in the liquid. The note heard is the frequency of standing wave with fixed wavelength of liquid column height.
title: Hot chocolate effect
description: Tap a mug while stirring in cocoa powder and the note drops sharply, then slowly climbs back as the froth clears: tiny air bubbles make the liquid springy and slow sound down enormously. Physicist Frank Crawford described it in 1982.
effect: a few bubbles in a liquid slow sound in it dramatically
usedIn: Bubble curtains that muffle offshore pile-driving noise to protect porpoises
US Navy 'Prairie-Masker' air systems that hide ship noise
strength: Just 1% air bubbles cuts the speed of sound in water from about 1,500 m/s to roughly 120 m/s.
pickWhy: Borderline: Sounds like a kitchen curiosity, but the underlying effect (bubbles slowing and blocking sound) is strong and used in bubble curtains; kept under its popular name, though Crawford popularised rather than discovered the physics (Wood worked out the theory around 1930).
